findings.passage: The version he corrected was the more flattering one, the whistleblower walking out on a powerful company. He did not want credit for a story that was not quite true.
findings.problem: The hook's moral reading is more flattering than the record supports. The NYT body (S04, opened from the cached Wayback copy) based its framing on Hinton's own statement: he 'said he did not want to publicly criticize Google or other companies until he had quit his job,' and he had just spoken with Sundar Pichai. So the tweet clarified an implication of his own words. It did not turn down undeserved credit. His 2025 account (S12, 01:15:49) gives a cheaper explanation: 'I didn't leave cuz I was cross with anything Google was doing. I think Google actually behaved very responsibly.' That explanation is ordinary accuracy plus goodwill toward an employer of ten years, at no cost to him. The same gloss comes back as fact later ('having left, he would not let Google be cast as the villain'), and 'It was the biggest stage he had ever had for a warning' has no source. This is item one of the discriminator, so the inflation carries into the type argument.
findings.acceptance_test: The opening says the Times was relaying his own line about not criticizing Google while employed. 'He did not want credit…' is either removed or marked as inference ('this suggests'), with goodwill toward Google named as the plain alternative. 'Biggest stage he had ever had' is sourced or cut. The Google-section sentence about the villain is framed as interpretation.

findings.passage: But his costliest choices follow a second rule, and it shows up far from AI: when Hinton decides something is wrong, he cannot leave it alone.
findings.problem: The standard asks for a motive that explains repeated costly choices, and the piece claims cost (also in the FAQ: 'often at a cost'). Most discriminator items cost him little or nothing. Correcting the Times cost nothing and pleased his former employer. By his own account, he left Google mainly because he was 75 and wanted to retire. The congressional briefing, the press conference and the Encode statement added to his standing. Even the Nobel promise ended with Sejnowski refusing the money and a prize in Sejnowski's name. The choices that plausibly were costly (refusing to sell the house for Rosalind's treatment; the 1987 move away from Pentagon-funded research, which the record excludes) are not the ones carrying the argument.
findings.acceptance_test: Either the body names at least two sourced choices where acting on the standard cost him something he valued (money, standing, a relationship, comfort) and ties them to the Type 1 case, or 'costliest' (body) and 'often at a cost' (FAQ) are replaced with wording the record supports, such as 'most telling' or 'most consistent'.

findings.passage: That could describe any stubborn genius. What makes it look like a One is the shape of the rightness. It has a "should" in it.
findings.problem: This rests on a play on the word 'should.' 'It should be true… If I was God, I'd make it true' is an aesthetic hope about an algorithm. Bengio's 'This should not work' is a prediction. Neither is a moral standard, and the evidence record says so itself (C28: 'The quotes are about algorithms, not morality; reading "should" as typological is interpretive'). The section then shows him dropping the 'should' for whatever works better, which is the Five's evidence-first move. The same slide happens earlier: 'The science that changed the world, by his own account, ran mostly on should' recasts his own words, 'mostly anxiety,' as a Type 1 term. Anxiety fits Six or Three at least as well (the record's 'against' admits this).
findings.acceptance_test: The section no longer treats a grammatical 'should' as evidence for Type 1. Either the aesthetic/predictive 'should' is named as fitting a Five's love of elegant models equally, or the paragraph is reframed as texture rather than discriminator. The father-section closing line keeps his own word ('anxiety') or explicitly labels the 'should' gloss as the author's.

findings.passage: Hinton does the opposite, across decades and domains.
findings.problem: The most obvious adverse evidence for 'cannot leave a wrong alone' is missing. Hinton stayed silent during ten years at Google, including Google's 2020 ouster of Timnit Gebru. Margaret Mitchell publicly criticized him for it in May 2023. When CNN asked about Gebru's critique, Hinton reportedly said those were 'rather different concerns from mine' and 'it's easier to voice concerns if you leave the company first.' A skeptic would bring this up first. It suggests his correcting reflex is selective and partly about where he is in his career. Limitation: I saw this only in search results (Fortune 2023-05-03 'ai-scientists-dire-warnings-mixed-opinions'; Daily Dot; an opinion piece), not in an opened source or the CNN transcript. It is not in the evidence record.
findings.acceptance_test: Research opens the CNN interview transcript (May 2023) and at least one report quoting Mitchell, then adds them as sources. The draft confronts the Google-era silence and Hinton's response near the Type 5 discriminator, in a sentence that states what it does to the Type 1 case, or the evidence record explains why it was rejected.

findings.passage: Curiosity explains why he studied the brain for fifty years. It does not explain the heat.
findings.problem: The closing line of the type argument depends on 'heat,' and that evidence is thin. 'Still enrage him' is Rothman's narration from one visit, not Hinton's words. 'That's just crazy' about unsafe drinking water is an ordinary moral reaction. 'It was just completely obvious to me' is certainty, not anger. Elsewhere the draft calls him dry, funny and guilt-free. In the Type 5 section, the author's own voice turns the reporter's adjective into fact ('the contractors' mistakes still make him angry'), and the type-answer section does the same ('contractors' mistakes that still enrage him').
findings.acceptance_test: Every anger statement is attributed to Rothman where it appears. Either the body adds at least one first-person or independently sourced example of anger at a wrong, or the closing line is softened to match the evidence (for example, 'It explains less well why he keeps acting on what he judges wrong').

findings.passage: The Five's characteristic move is to understand it and conserve himself, staying out of the fray.
findings.problem: Both rivals are tested against weak versions. Many Fives are relentless public critics (Chomsky is in this page's own suggestions). Hinton wanted to retire, lives on an island and says he is 'very good at ignoring what other people say,' all of which fits Five withdrawal. The Six is dismissed in one line ('a Six tends to test certainty against allies and authorities') without addressing the counterphobic Six. That Six is contrarian and self-certain, and it fits his stated security motive for selling DNNresearch (his son 'would never be out on the street'), the three banks and 'mostly anxiety.' The better discriminator is already in the draft: he calls the advocacy a 'duty' and says criticizing while paid 'just feels wrong'.
findings.acceptance_test: The Five comparison is framed by motive (understanding vs. obligation) and anchored on his own 'duty' / 'feels wrong' words, not on Fives staying out of public life. The Six paragraph names the counterphobic version and the security-driven sale, and gives one sourced reason the Six reading falls short.

findings.passage: Then, of AI: "We can't be in denial," he said. "We have to be real."
findings.problem: The quote is accurate, but the New Yorker context (S01) cuts against the thesis and is left out. Hinton framed the lesson from his wives' deaths as 'There are two approaches to A.I. There's denial, and there's stoicism,' and Rothman adds that 'it was important to recognize when cutting it out was just a fantasy.' His own takeaway is stoic acceptance of what can't be fixed, which is close to the opposite of 'cannot leave it alone.' The paragraph's lead-in ('His grief has a line running through it') borrows 'I drew the line' to suggest a corrective reflex.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph includes the denial-versus-stoicism framing (in Hinton's words) and says how it fits or strains the Type 1 reading, preferably within 'What the One reading leaves out'.

findings.passage: He does change his mind when the facts change.
findings.problem: The draft presents his move from 'I've never recommended slowing the advancement of AI' (October 2024) to 'We need to slow down' (September 16, 2026) as updating on evidence. It never says what facts changed. The 2026 remark came after a briefing organized by Bernie Sanders, so audience and occasion are also possible explanations. The flattering causal story is assumed, not shown.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph either cites what Hinton said changed his view, or presents the shift as an unexplained reversal and labels the 'facts change' reading as inference.

protected_passages.passage: That is a man managing how he looks to buyers, a point for image (Type 3), not for Type 1.
protected_passages.reason: The draft brings in adverse evidence on its own and scores it against its thesis. This is the honesty the critic role looks for.

protected_passages.passage: Both lines are Metz's narration, not Hinton's words.
protected_passages.reason: Clean separation of reconstruction from quotation at the point where it matters most.

protected_passages.passage: Duty without guilt is a real pattern, but it is not the self-punishing One of the textbooks.
protected_passages.reason: Names a real contradiction the type does not explain, without explaining it away with a wing.

protected_passages.passage: Two years later he gave a fuller and less heroic account to Steven Bartlett.
protected_passages.reason: Puts the less flattering self-report (age, retirement) ahead of the heroic one. Keep it even if finding critic-01 changes the hook.

protected_passages.passage: And just near the door there was a slightly smaller box that simply said, 'Not insects,' and that's where he had all the things about the family.
protected_passages.reason: A specific, verified detail that does more than any summary of the father could.

assessment: Fair-minded skeptic's read: the draft is more honest about counterevidence than most. It gives Type 3 the humidifier episode, separates Metz's narration from Hinton's words, puts the less heroic retirement account first, and has a full section on what the One reading misses. The weak point is the discriminator. Its items are presented as costly, repeated corrections, but most cost him little (findings 1 and 2). The 'should' and 'heat' evidence is a word play and one reporter's adjective (findings 3 and 5). The most obvious skeptic's counterexample, ten silent years at Google including the Gebru ouster, is missing (finding 4, seen only in search results, not opened). The Type 1 lead may survive, but medium confidence currently rests on the weaker half of the evidence. Quotes I checked against cached copies (NYT, New Yorker, DOAC 01:14:55-01:15:52) match. Similarity: the two trips match the body-triad sentence ('three types organized around anger') against Aaron Pierre and Daniela Amodei. That is ordinary type vocabulary, and the arguments do not overlap, so it is not reported as reuse. Risk flags: contested typing (a credible Five/Six case) and sensitive material (his opinion of Altman as a living person, his late wife's medical choices) both stay set.
